Hindley–Milner type notation
Hindley–Milner signatures in JavaScript: how to read a -> b -> c and (a, b) -> c, type variables, [a] and Maybe a, and write a function from its signature.
Learn to read Hindley–Milner signatures — which arguments a function takes, what it returns and whether it is curried — and to write a function from its signature.

You have already come across Hindley–Milner type notation in the code — above functions, in comment blocks.
This type notation is used in Haskell and other languages with a functional bent. In JS it helps us write more abstract code, and it also helps maintain that code.
It explains which argument types a function accepts and what it returns.
code
Hindley–Milner notation in a comment above a function explains which argument types the function accepts and what it returns. In JS it helps write more abstract code and maintain it.

From the code (a, b) => a + b you can't tell whether the function adds numbers or concatenates strings. The signatures add :: (Number, Number) -> Number and concat :: (String, String) -> String tell you.
a -> b -> c is a curried function: it takes a and returns a function b -> c. For an uncurried function, the argument types are listed in parentheses, separated by commas: (a, b) -> c.
a, b, c are type variables: any type, but within a single signature the same letter always means the same type. [a] is an array of values of type a, Maybe a is a value of type a or its absence.

Write the functions from the signatures in the starter. between takes a lower bound, an upper bound and a number, and tells whether the number lies between them, inclusive. countWhere takes a predicate and an array and returns how many elements match the predicate. The signature of between shows that between(18)(65) is already a Number -> Boolean predicate.
